blocks.text: Imagine sending a letter across the globe, passing through various post offices before reaching its destination. In computer networks, routing plays a similar role, ensuring data packets find their way across multiple hops to reach the correct host.

blocks.markdown: Routing is a fundamental function of the network layer, responsible for determining the path that data packets take from a source to a destination across interconnected networks. This unit explores key routing algorithms and techniques used in modern networks.

blocks.title: Forwarding Table
blocks.text: A forwarding table, also known as a routing table, is used by routers to determine the next hop for a packet based on its destination address.

blocks.markdown: Routers use forwarding tables to make decisions about where to send packets next. The decision is based on the longest prefix match, which means the router selects the route with the most specific match to the destination IP address.

blocks.title: Longest Prefix Match
blocks.prompt: Determine the next hop for the destination IP address 192.168.1.45 using the following forwarding table:

steps.text:
1. Examine the forwarding table entries: 
- 192.168.1.0/24 via Next Hop A 
- 192.168.0.0/16 via Next Hop B 
- 0.0.0.0/0 via Next Hop C
2. Compare the destination IP 192.168.1.45 with each entry to find the longest prefix match.
3. The longest prefix match is 192.168.1.0/24, which directs the packet to Next Hop A.

blocks.markdown: Routing protocols are used to build and maintain forwarding tables. Two common types are Distance Vector and Link State routing protocols.

blocks.title: Distance Vector Routing
blocks.text: Distance Vector Routing is a protocol where each router maintains a table (vector) of minimum distances to every destination and shares this information with its neighbors.

blocks.title: Link State Routing
blocks.text: Link State Routing involves routers having a complete map of the network topology, allowing them to compute the shortest path to every destination independently.

blocks.caption: Comparison of Distance Vector and Link State Routing Protocols

blocks.title: Convergence of Distance Vector Protocol
blocks.prompt: Trace the convergence of a distance vector protocol after a link failure between Router A and Router B.

steps.text: 1. Router A detects the link failure and updates its distance vector, setting the distance to Router B as infinity.
2. Router A shares its updated distance vector with its neighbors.
3. Neighbors update their distance vectors based on the new information and share with their neighbors.
4. This process continues until all routers have updated their distance vectors, reflecting the new topology.

blocks.answer: The network converges when all routers have updated their distance vectors to reflect the link failure.

blocks.title: Routing Protocol Convergence
blocks.text: Distance Vector protocols converge slowly due to incremental updates, while Link State protocols converge quickly due to complete topology awareness.

points: Routing is essential for directing packets across networks using forwarding tables.
Longest prefix match is used to determine the next hop in forwarding tables.
Distance Vector and Link State are two primary routing protocols, each with unique characteristics and trade-offs.
